doc.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: A failed Aquarius-style chart and Bones Howe
summary: A singer's Aquarius-style opener flopped; Bones Howe won union acceptance as a mixer.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay, here’s a hard question. Have you ever had an occasion where you wrote something that came out just really badly, and the person you wrote it for said, “hey, no thanks, this doesn’t work at all”?

Yeah, yeah. It was for a singer. I think they heard the thing that The Fifth Dimension did, “Aquarius,” and they wanted a feeling like that. And they wanted it for an opener, and I did what I thought was it, and they took it on the road someplace. I don’t know how these other players played it, again, my not being there to explain it might have made the difference, but they said it was a total egg.
So are you responsible for the age of “Aquarius,” the [scats] all that introduction stuff in that chart?
Was he the guy? Was he easy to get along with? Was he a good producer for you?

Yeah. He came on the scene in the 50s when the west coast jazz thing was going along. I mean he was such a good mixer, he hadn’t had enough work yet to be accepted into the union, so the union didn’t want him to be a mixer. They actually didn’t want him at the board and all the musicians insisted on it so they finally gave him some kind of an internship or something like that, where he was able to do that. And then he turns around to be a hot pop producer.
